chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man has a large quantity of dried grapes (busr) as a debt owed to him, and he takes from it a large quantity of fresh dates (rutab) in place of it, and the fresh dates are less in quantity than the dried grapes. He said: 'There is no objection.' I said: And if he has a large quantity of dried grapes owed to him, and he takes from it a large quantity of dried dates (tamr), and the dried dates are more in quantity than the dried grapes. He said: 'There is no objection if that is well-known/customary between you two.'

key_terms.بُسْرٌ: Dried grapes (a type of dried fruit)
key_terms.جُلَّةٌ: A large quantity or bulk amount

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for repaying a debt with a different type of food item if the quantities differ?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the flexibility in *qard* (interest-free loan) repayment by allowing the substitution of different date varieties, provided the exchange is mutually recognized (*ma'rufan*). It highlights the Shia juristic principle that customary practice (*urf*) validates variations in quantity and type, distinguishing this from strict *riba* prohibitions when the intent is debt settlement rather than profit. This underscores the practical adaptability of Islamic finance in historical trade contexts.
